title: Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles announces she's cancer-free
description: White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has announced she is free of cancer, exactly six months after she announced her diagnosis. In a post on X, Wile
body: White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has announced she is free of cancer, exactly six months after she announced her diagnosis. In a post on X, Wiles said her pathology tests "came back clear" after a visit to the Mayo Clinic earlier this week. Wiles, 69, is considered among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president. In her post, Wiles thanked Trump for his "unwavering support" and vowed to continue working to "advance his America First Agenda". Wiles continued working virtually at the White House during the six months of treatment following her diagnosis.In a March statement, Wiles said that one in eight women are diagnosed with breast cancer."Every day, these women continue to raise their families, go to work and serve their communities with strength and determination," she said. "I now join their ranks."Her post on Wednesday did not reveal any more details about her treatment.Wiles is the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff - widely considered to be the most important role in the White House.In her position, Wiles works to keep the president's agenda on track and serves as a gatekeeper to President Trump, as well as a policy coordinator and political advisor.Before taking the job, Wiles played a significant role in President Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.Her tenure, however, has not been without controversy.In December, Vanity Fair published interviews with Wiles in which she gave a blunt - and occasionally unflattering - assessment of her time working in the Trump White House.For example, she described the famously teetotaling president as having an "alcoholic's personality" but added that there's "nothing he can't do. Nothing, zero, nothing."She also provided candid thoughts about other figures close to the US president, describing Vice-President JD Vance as a "conspiracy theorist" and Elon Musk as an "odd, odd duck."The US president, however, swiftly came to her defence and Wiles described Vanity Fair's reporting as having omitted "significant context" to create a "chaotic and negative narrative" about the administration.President Trump and the White House have yet to comment on Wiles' announcement.

schema.headline: Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles announces she's cancer-free

title: Hyrox athlete apologises for continuing race after soiling herself
description: After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win.Wietrzyk said in a social media post: "I want to offer my si
body: After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win.Wietrzyk said in a social media post: "I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing."She wrote in a social media post, external that she was "completely fit and healthy" at the start of the race, and had "no reason" to expect any illness."Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused," Wietrzyk continued.Hyrox insisted it had "clear biocontaminant and medical procedures in place".It said "an unforeseen situation arose" during which protocols became blurred, "creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".In a statement posted on Instagram, Fürste committed to "improving event processes" to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

schema.headline: Hyrox athlete apologises for continuing race after soiling herself

title: US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt of Congress
description: The US House of Representatives has agreed to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying a legal summons related to its investiga
body: The US House of Representatives has agreed to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying a legal summons related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Black, who had business ties to Epstein, did not comply with a subpoena ordering him to appear before the House Oversight Committee earlier this month and share documents related to Epstein. Lawyers for Black, who has sued over the summons, called the contempt move "outrageous".After passage of the measure holding Black in contempt, Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said: "No-one is above the law. We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors."In a statement shared with US media, lawyers for Black called the House move an "outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr Black"."The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee's actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer," they said.The measure, which passed by unanimous consent, means the matter will be referred to the US justice department, which will decide whether to criminally prosecute Black. In a written statement, the committee's top Democrat, congressman Robert Garcia, called the contempt vote "an important step towards justice and accountability". "We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes," he said. The private equity tycoon walked out of voluntary testimony before the House Oversight Committee in June after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time.Black left Apollo Global Management, which he co-founded, amid scrutiny in 2021 over his Epstein ties. He has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein.The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June.Black has said he hired Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling lawmakers in June that he gave Epstein $158m (£118m) for legitimate reasons. The billionaire has said he did not know about Epstein's crimes until he was charged with sex trafficking in July 2019.

schema.headline: US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt of Congress

title: Australia immigration crackdown: visas for international students and backpackers targeted
description: International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will be targeted under stricter rules announced by Australia on Thursday in a bid to
body: International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will be targeted under stricter rules announced by Australia on Thursday in a bid to curb immigration.Foreign students will no longer be able to bring their families with them and those who want to extend their stay must choose a higher qualification.Rules will also be stricter for working holiday visas - commonly used by backpackers and a crucial labour source for the agricultural sector - with a ballot system although these changes will not affect the UK.The new rules were revealed by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke who said that while immigration was a "strength" of Australia, there needed to be a "high level of control".For international student and graduate visas, Burke said: "We will no longer be adding to the stock of students automatically being able to bring family members over."There would be exemptions for foreign students already in Australia as well as applicants from the Pacific and South East Asian countries, he said.PhD students would also be able to bring their families as they were in different life circumstances to undergraduates, Burke said. In a speech titled "The work of managing the migration program: who arrives, who stays, who leaves", Burke revealed a raft of changes as the government aims to bring net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.On student visas, he said the government would clamp down on "visa hopping" - where a student finishes a course, then applies to do another course which is often a lower qualification and sometimes with a "not so legitimate provider".Students who want to go "up the scale" will be allowed, Burke said, for example, if a student finishes a bachelor's degree and then wants to complete a masters.He also announced major changes to working holiday visas for those aged 18 to 30 years old who can work in Australia for 12 months, but can extend for a second and third year. Currently, these visa holders must work for three months in regional Australia during their first year to qualify for a second year, and then six months to qualify for a third year.Under the new changes, those who qualify for a second year will have to go into a ballot with a cap of 45,000, down from the 57,000 who qualified last year.For the third year, the ballot will be limited to 5,000, down from 31,000 who qualified last year. British working holidaymakers will not be affected by these changes due to the UK's free trade agreement with Australia.New figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday showed Australia's population grew 1.4% in the 12 months to March 2026 to 27.9m.That total figure included births and deaths as well as a net overseas migration of 292,100. Migration remains a major political issue as debate around Australia's population grows amid rising living costs, housing affordability and increased strain on public services.One Nation, a populist right-wing party known for its anti-immigration stance and which has seen a surge in support in recent months, detailed its migration policy earlier this week, proposing to cut temporary migrant visas by 750,000 over three years.The party, which won its first lower house seat in May, also wants to cap net overseas immigration to 130,000, drawing a rebuke from Burke who said such a proposal would risk "smashing parts of the Australian economy".In July, the government introduced a policy to prioritise applications for family visas  lodged onshore - where the applicant is in the country already - over those submitted overseas. Skilled migrants already in Australia who applied for permanent visas were also prioritised over those applying from overseas.It also paused applications for working holiday visas from 24 countries, not including the UK.Violet Roumeliotis, from Settlement Services International which helps new arrivals to Australia, says the migration debate was increasingly driven by "short-term politics rather than what is best for the country". "The proposed changes to family visas for international students is a good example of this," she said, adding that it would make it harder for Australia to compete for "future talent".

schema.headline: Australia immigration crackdown: visas for international students and backpackers targeted

title: Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees
description: Figure caption, Watch: Is Canada about to join the EU?ByKatya AdlerEurope editorIs Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot
body: Figure caption, Watch: Is Canada about to join the EU?ByKatya AdlerEurope editorIs Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot of confusion right now.The EU constitution rules that possibility out as Canada is geographically outside Europe.But in a speech on Thursday to the European Parliament, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities."Mark Carney was responding – extremely warmly – to an invitation by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for Canada to become the EU's first associate member.The EU and Canada already have a far-reaching trade deal (Ceta) in place but Carney insisted additional cooperation on energy and economic security, on critical and raw materials, education, tech and AI innovation, and defence would help safeguard all countries involved.Canada and the EU feel increasingly squeezed by the superpowers USA on the one side and China on the other – and by tech giants, too, that seem to operate supranationally.The idea of associate EU membership, Carney emphasised, would not be to form a third superpower or to create a bloc against anyone else."We do not pursue zero sum deals," he said. Instead he suggested like-minded nations should club together to create a new form of multilateral global governance in an increasingly turbulent world where – in the minds of some others - might is right.Only by countries joining forces and shunning isolationism, Carney suggested, could they close key capability gaps, build strength and ensure national sovereignty.This last may have been a nod to upcoming elections across Europe and the continent's increasingly powerful nationalist politicians. Their slogans – whether "Italy First" or "France for the French" or "Make Poland Great Again" – echo Donald Trump's call to Make America Great Again.Carney's words were hopeful and warm; the applause in the European Parliament rapturous and apparently heartfelt.Not so across the Atlantic. On Wednesday, Donald Trump dismissed the EU associate membership proposal out of hand, threatened to impose "very heavy tariffs" if the agreement came to fruition and warned he may view it as a "hostile act".But the US president is the unintentional matchmaker for this EU-Canada love-in.Traditionally, America is trade partner and defence ally number one for Canada and the EU. But Ottawa is currently embroiled in what it calls an escalating trade "war" with the White House. Both Canada and the EU have been stung by what they view as Washington's weaponisation of trade tariffs. They also fear they can no longer fully rely on the US to have their back in terms of security and defence.Figure caption, Watch: 'A better opportunity' - Canadians on a closer alliance with EuropeCanada is not alone among Europe's far-flung allies, now seeking to cosy closer to the EU, as they worry the US is becoming too unpredictable a partner. Japan and South Korea show an interest in sheltering under the EU umbrella too.For its part, the EU has recently hastened to secure a list of trade deals – with India, Indonesia and Japan for example – to intentionally diversify relationships.But there is no guarantee Canada's associate membership of the EU will ever get off the ground, never mind become a blueprint for other countries, like the UK wanting closer relations stopping short of full EU membership.Any deal would have to be approved by each one of the EU's 27 countries.No legal precedent exists, negotiations would be lengthy and potential conflicts of interest loom, over steel tariffs for example.A suggestion in May by Germany to make Ukraine – a country desperate for full membership of the European Union as soon as possible – an associate member was rejected by others in the EU.Some, including France's government, want to avoid EU non-members securing "too good" a deal. They fear eurosceptic forces at home and abroad could then encourage voters to clamour to leave the bloc.In the end, "associate membership" is just a label. Buffeted by adverse winds – from China, the US and Russia, the normally rigid rules-based EU is coming under serious pressure to show more flexibility in accommodating countries wanting to stand by its side.

schema.headline: Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees

title: US to allow Iran delegation to attend UN meetings in New York
description: The US government has granted visas to Iranian officials so they can travel to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, as the war between the t
body: The US government has granted visas to Iranian officials so they can travel to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, as the war between the two countries grinds into its seventh month. The BBC understands the core delegation permitted to attend includes Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.A spokesman for the US State Department confirmed the decision on Thursday, saying that the delegation will be placed under travel restrictions and will be banned from purchasing certain American products. The move comes as the war shows no sign of ending. Since it began in February, it has driven up global energy prices, and expanded into neighbouring countries."Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week," a spokesman for the US State Department told the BBC. "The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year."Last year, diplomats attending from Iran were banned from shopping at wholesale stores like Costco. They also were required to seek permission from the US before purchasing luxury goods, including jewellery, alcohol and cars. State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott said the US would prevent the diplomats from "going on shopping sprees" as the Iranian people deal with water and electricity shortages, "brutal repression", and "soaring inflation"."We will not let the Iranian regime's elites exploit UNGA for a luxury retail splurge paid for by the Iranian people's suffering, all while the regime funnels Iran's wealth to support its terrorist proxies," he posted on X, warning New York shops to "be on guard" against selling goods to the delegation.He did not indicate if the US was aware of any specific plans from the delegation to buy luxury items.The 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) is currently underway. The General Debate - the centrepiece of the annual event - is due to begin on Tuesday.Tuesday will include speeches from US President Donald Trump, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and France President Emmanuel Macron.Wednesday is expected to see speeches from the leaders of Ukraine, Syria and Iran.Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.Since the war began, Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.The BBC recently learned that the US denied a visa to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and the Palestinian delegation to attend UNGA.The White House, which does not recognise the legitimacy of the Palestinian delegation, denied them visas for a second year in a row.

schema.headline: US to allow Iran delegation to attend UN meetings in New York

title: Aztec document goes on display in Mexico after 186 years
description: In return, Mexico has agreed to lend another priceless document, the Codex Boturini, to France for display there. The pictograms in the Codex Boturini
body: In return, Mexico has agreed to lend another priceless document, the Codex Boturini, to France for display there. The pictograms in the Codex Boturini narrate the story of the migration of the Aztecs, also known as Mexica, from their ancestral homeland to the shores of Lake Texcoco, where they built Tenochtitlán.The temporary exchange of the two codices was agreed by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and her French counterpart, Emmanuel Macron, during a visit by the latter to Mexico last year. Mexico has long lobbied for the return of historical artefacts taken from the country in past centuries.According to Mexico's ministry of foreign relations, last year more than 2,000 objects were successfully repatriated. The Codex Azcatitlán will be exhibited at the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City from Thursday.

schema.headline: Aztec document goes on display in Mexico after 186 years

title: Austin Tice: Assad regime planned US journalist's kidnap for weeks, BBC finds
description: US journalist Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria in 2012, was kidnapped in a calculated operation which was more than a month in the planning, the
body: US journalist Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria in 2012, was kidnapped in a calculated operation which was more than a month in the planning, the BBC can reveal. A member of the group which detained Tice has also claimed the abduction was sanctioned by Syria's leader at the time, President Bashar al-Assad.Tice was seen getting into a car with a driver he knew and trusted. For years, many assumed they had stumbled upon a government checkpoint, and that the abduction of the journalist had been opportunistic. But we have uncovered evidence that, in fact, his disappearance was anything but chance.In a new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, we reveal the findings of a years-long investigation into what happened to Tice, who had been reporting on Syria's civil war at the time. His case has been followed closely by international media and cited by successive US presidents.Georgetown University law student Tice, who had served as a US Marines captain, was last seen in a video - blindfolded and in apparent distress - posted more than a month after his capture.As the regime fell 12 years later, tens of thousands of people emerged from the administration's prisons. Tice was not one of them. We obtained co-ordinates from an intelligence source for multiple locations US authorities suspected he could have been held at, and searched for him for more than a month, but found no sign of him.A former Syrian commander has said Tice was executed. Others have questioned this account and no remains have been found.But in the aftermath of the regime's collapse, we did uncover secret Syrian intelligence files on Tice - hundreds of pages of internal records providing the first definitive proof that it was the regime that had held the journalist.Two crucial questions remained unanswered, however: how exactly had Tice been taken in the first place? And, who was responsible for his abduction?We have spoken to a number of men from the regime involved in Tice's detention, and have reviewed recordings of discussions about it. One man we spoke to, Abu Ali, is a former member of the National Defence Forces (NDF), a militia which was fiercely loyal to Assad.He says the abduction operation began when Tice's driver - who multiple sources say had been passing the regime information for some time - told a senior NDF member that Tice was moving through rebel-held areas, reporting on the opposition.Tice had pushed into areas most journalists deemed too dangerous and was writing front-page stories for the Washington Post. The Assad regime was cracking down on anyone highlighting its human rights abuses.We have been told the NDF member Tice's driver spoke to was Sakr Rustom - not just any NDF militia contact, but nephew of Bassam al-Hassan, one of Assad's most trusted security figures and head of the NDF.The information on Tice was passed up to Hassan, Abu Ali says, who is then said to have telephoned Assad."Bring him to us," Assad replied, claims Abu Ali.Abu Ali says he was subsequently called into Hassan's office and told the president had approved the operation.But Tice was not taken immediately. The driver, Abu Ali says, suggested that he and the NDF continue watching him, to uncover more about what he was doing."He trusts me," Abu Ali recalls the driver saying.Some time later, the driver reported back that Tice's actions seemed suspicious, Abu Ali says. Tice, as a trained marine, would sometimes share his military experience with rebel fighters - according to several people we spoke to - and would correct fighters on how they used their weapons.To the men watching him, that behaviour made Tice look less like a journalist and more like someone from the CIA. The BBC has found no evidence to suggest this was the case, and a former senior US official responsible for part of Tice's case has denied he was an intelligence officer.In the days before Tice vanished, the driver made one particularly brazen move while Tice was interviewing rebel fighters. He secretly took the American's backpack, containing his MacBook, a satellite transmitter and other personal items, for regime operatives to look through, multiple sources say.On 11 August 2012, Tice celebrated his 31st birthday at a rebel safehouse on the western edge of Damascus, a few miles from Assad's presidential palace. There was a swimming pool, Free Syrian Army fighters, Taylor Swift music and whiskey, Tice revealed in what would become his final tweet."Hands down, best birthday ever," he wrote.Then came the time for Tice to leave Syria. He had told various people he was planning to take time out in Lebanon.But he was not heading to safety. He was heading to a state facility where Hassan had an office, in an area called Tahouneh on the outskirts of Damascus, according to several sources. Abu Ali was waiting there for Tice.Abu Ali says Tice's driver told him that when he drew up to the gates, he pulled out a gun.Tice laughed at first, Ali recalls the driver saying, apparently believing the man he trusted was joking. But the driver told Tice he was serious, Abu Ali says, and the journalist realised what was happening. According to Ali, Tice pulled out his chequebook and pleaded with the driver to name his price, rather than go through with the kidnap.NDF militia members then grabbed Tice, covering his eyes, Abu Ali says. Another NDF member told us he would never forget Tice's expression as he realised he had been betrayed. Abu Ali says Hassan immediately called President Assad to tell him they had the American.For years, the identity of Tice's driver has remained a mystery.The BBC spoke to more than 20 people to discover who he was, with the trail eventually leading to the city of Homs, and the family of a man called Hamid Abu Obeid.They confirmed he was the man who had driven Tice away, an account also supported by multiple NDF members. But by the time we identified him, Abu Obeid had disappeared. His family say they do not know where he is, and fear for his safety. They say they were not aware of Hamid's involvement in Tice's case, and learned about it from him afterwards.But they did give a motive for his betrayal of Tice.The Abu Obeid family, Palestinian refugees from Gaza, live in poverty. Under Syrian law they are not entitled to Syrian citizenship and live under significant restrictions. According to Hamid's brother, he had been promised a passport, Syrian citizenship, a house, and a weapon, in return for delivering Tice - life-changing rewards. But after the abduction, the family says all he got was a pistol.Then, after Assad's regime fell, Abu Obeid's wife says her husband was called by a man who knew about his involvement in Tice's case and was threatening to tell the US embassy, hoping it might help him secure asylum. Abu Obeid urged him not to. He then took some money, told his wife he was going shopping, and she says she has not seen him since. She does not know if he is in hiding, or if he has been detained or killed.Not long after he disappeared, she says masked men - some dressed in military clothes - visited and took a number of Abu Obeid's possessions, including his laptop and other devices.The wishes of Abu Obeid's wife now chillingly mirror those of Tice's mother and family. On opposite sides of a disappearance that began more than a decade ago, both families are searching for the same thing: a loved one who vanished, and an answer to where he went.

schema.headline: Austin Tice: Assad regime planned US journalist's kidnap for weeks, BBC finds

title: EU announces plan to restrict social media access for children
description: The EU has announced plans to restrict social media access for under-15s across its member states, in a bid to increase wellbeing and tackle online sa
body: The EU has announced plans to restrict social media access for under-15s across its member states, in a bid to increase wellbeing and tackle online safety.Under the plans, there would be a gradual approach to children using social media which would include banning under 13s from accessing platforms.Those aged 13 to 15 would only be able to access platforms for an hour per day via "mini accounts" set up through their parent or guardian's social media account.The European Commission said social media companies would need to prove platforms were safe by design or face fines of up to 6% of their global sales. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the move would "put parents back in the driving seat". She added the legislation - called the EU Kids Act - would give parents "the tools to help their children navigate a safer world".The restrictions would not just affect well-known apps such as TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat but also YouTube and other video sharing platforms as well as AI chatbots and online games."Too many children are being exposed too early to an online world they are not ready to navigate - an environment where bullying can follow you home, where every mistake can be recorded forever," von der Leyen said.Under the act, only children aged 15 and over would be able to set up their own social media accounts.But von der Leyen told the EU Parliament on Thursday that "an age limit does not mean letting tech companies off the hook for the content on the platform".She added that under the legislation - if it is approved - companies would be required to submit detailed child safety plans. "For every person under 18, the platforms must follow the principle of safety by design, no toxic or addictive features, no traps, etc," she said.Some individual EU countries have already announced their own plans to restrict social media for children, including France and Spain.The proposed EU-wide legislation would supersede those, and member states will not be able to opt out from what would be a legally binding regulation.It is understood the Commission has warned some member states they would need  to repeal any national laws passed before the EU Kids Act comes into effect.The new plans need to be agreed by EU member states and approved by the European Parliament.Already there are questions about how this EU-wide legislation would be enforced and the plans are likely to face opposition in the months to come.France provides an indication of how the path ahead could be bumpy as individual member states may try to strengthen or weaken the proposals.The Macron government drew up legislation for a ban on social media for under-15s but last month the country's top court blocked it, ruling that it infringed upon freedom of expression.French ministers have now amended their original plans.Some critics of social media bans for children cite privacy concerns.They worry about teenagers being forced to submit personal information as they go through an age verification process to prove they are old enough to access platforms.The Commission has said age would be verified using the EU's preexisting age verification app, and no personal data would be collected or shared.Social media companies will also make their position on the restrictions clear as the act is debated in the months to come. Von der Leyen had previously proposed a social media "delay" for children in Europe,  saying in May that "the discussion about a minimum age for social media can no longer be ignored".The policy, formally outlined on Thursday, was also trailed in the EU chief's annual address on Wednesday.In July, the EU said Meta must change the "addictive" design of Facebook and Instagram or face a heavy fine.In preliminary findings, the European Commission said features such as infinite scroll, autoplaying videos and personalised recommendations could encourage "compulsive use", particularly among children and teens.A spokesperson for the tech giant told the BBC it disagreed with the findings "which don't accurately take into account the significant steps we've taken to protect teens".In a separate case, Meta agreed in August to a $18bn (£13.3bn) settlement with US states and territories to resolve claims that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. It denied any wrongdoing as part of the settlement.The European Commission said its proposed legislation built on findings, external from its special panel on child safety online, which recommended age-appropriate regulation for children, with different guidance for each age group.It also cited recent EU survey data, external, which found 92% of respondents considered the need to strengthen children's protection online as a top policy priority. Von der Leyen said the Commission had "looked at Australia" - which banned social media platforms for under-16s last year - when putting together the proposal.The ban has been difficult for the country to enforce, with its Communications Minister Anika Wells admitting earlier this month that so far no tech firm had been fined despite research showing many under-16s were still on platforms.A similar ban for under-16s is set to come into force in the UK in spring next year.

schema.headline: EU announces plan to restrict social media access for children

title: Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member'
description: Canada and the US are locked in an escalating trade dispute, with each side imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after bilateral talks collapsed last month."T
body: Canada and the US are locked in an escalating trade dispute, with each side imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after bilateral talks collapsed last month."Today our societies are being battered by new storms," Carney said during his address, naming them as climate change, "the erosion of democratic norms" and the "weaponisation of trade"."Economic integration is now being weaponised, tariffs being used to exert pressure," he said."Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited."He said a Canada-EU alliance would create a "beacon for other democracies", while stressing the two sides were not seeking to form a new power bloc."I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival - only with better manners," he told MEPs."This is about sovereignty, our ability to live as we wish. We do not seek power to dominate others."Asked about the proposal on Wednesday, Trump told reporters: "If I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things."If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility." Responding to Trump's comments at a press conference following his address, Carney said: "This alliance is a positive process, that's my response to the American president.""Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak, no-one is going to dictate our culture, or with whom we can strike agreements internationally," he added.Carney said Canada was "not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member of the European Union", describing the proposal as a "different framework".Speaking at the European Parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said she wanted Canada to become the EU's first associate member, with closer cooperation in areas such as manufacturing, technology, defence, energy critical minerals and economic security.It is unclear exactly what that relationship would look like because the "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement.Any new arrangement would require the agreement of all 27 EU member states, with some governments having previously expressed reservations about creating a new form of membership. The EU and Canada already have a free-trade agreement, and cooperate in areas including trade, defence and research.In his address, Carney said Canada and Europe could strengthen their "strategic autonomy" through "deep co-operation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals".He said Canada could supply liquefied natural gas and hydrogen to support European energy security, while benefiting from Europe's expertise in clean-energy technologies.He also proposed pooling technological resources and deepening "people to people ties", including allowing young people to "work, study and live where they want on either side of the Atlantic" through Canada joining the EU's Erasmus+ programme.Carney described the proposed relationship as "a unique, positive approach that we will define together".He added that there would be a debate and a vote in the Canadian parliament on the proposals, but emphasised the two sides were still at the "start of a road".A Canada-EU summit is due to take place in Montreal at the end of October, where Carney said they would "drill down the details".

schema.headline: Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member'

title: One dead after torrential rain and flash floods hit Barcelona region
description: North-eastern Spain has been hit by torrential rain and flash floods, leaving one person dead and causing widespread disruption across the region.Spai
body: North-eastern Spain has been hit by torrential rain and flash floods, leaving one person dead and causing widespread disruption across the region.Spain's national weather agency AEMET issued warnings for heavy rain across eastern regions on Wednesday, including a red alert for Barcelona's coastline.Rescuers recovered the body of a man on Thursday in Olivella, around 40km (25 miles) west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away by a stream, authorities said.The deluge has disrupted travel across Catalonia and Valencia, with flights cancelled and roads submerged. Authorities have advised against unnecessary travel, while Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez warned of "very complicated situations".Emergency services in Catalonia said they received more than 850 calls related to the downpours and catalogued over 500 incidents.Catalan firefighters said on X on Thursday that they had recovered the "lifeless body of a man" in Olivella, correcting earlier reports that had identified the missing person as a woman.Videos shared on social media showed partially submerged cars and rescue workers attempting to reach a vehicle trapped in a heavily flooded underpass.In Barcelona, some metro stations were closed and buses diverted, while regional trains were disrupted and flights delayed or cancelled at El Prat airport.Neighbouring Valencia had more than 70mm (2.76in) of rain fall in just half an hour in several municipalities, according to AVAMET."Rarely have we seen such rainfall accumulations in 30 minutes," the meteorological association said on X.Emergency services reported 478 incidents in the Valencia province, mostly involving property damage, leaks and traffic disruption. In the regional capital, all metro lines were suspended and the city's airport shuttered for several hours, causing flights to be diverted.

schema.headline: One dead after torrential rain and flash floods hit Barcelona region

title: Owen Ndlovu: Abducted South African journalist found dead with gunshot wounds
description: Provincial police spokesperson Col Dimakatso Nevhuhulwi said Ndlovu had gone to pick up his wife from a religious service when the attackers struck."A
body: Provincial police spokesperson Col Dimakatso Nevhuhulwi said Ndlovu had gone to pick up his wife from a religious service when the attackers struck."As she approached their vehicle, three unknown men, one reportedly armed with a firearm, suddenly approached them, pushed her aside and forced her husband into the back seat," she said."The suspects then drove off with the victim."The vehicle, a Ford Raptor pick-up truck - commonly known as a bakkie in South Africa - was later recovered abandoned in Walkerville, an area south of Johannesburg, police said.Ndlovu's body was found by local residents beside a road in Thokoza, which neighbours Katlehong. They said he appeared to have suffered gunshot wounds. A bag of his was found a few metres away.Police said they were investigating a case of murder but a post-mortem examination would establish the cause of death."At this stage, the family is awaiting further information from the relevant authorities regarding the circumstances surrounding Owen's death," said family spokesperson Eugene Mthethwa.The family described the loss as "devastating" and thanked residents, police and members of the public who had helped search for him after news of his abduction emerged.Ndlovu was a familiar figure to South African sports fans after years working as a presenter and producer at the SABC.He was also involved in radio coverage of the country's Premier Soccer League and later became an advocate for musicians' rights and royalty payments. The 54-year-old was also associated with Artists United and the SABC Summer Song of the Year initiative.Lelo Mzaca, a fellow journalist, remembered him as a man who lived a "colourful, energetic life" and brought enthusiasm and flair to sports broadcasting."South Africa has lost a unique and spirited individual whose light shone brightly while it lasted," Mzaca added in a tribute on the Mail & Guardian news site.The provincial government urged communities to help police with the investigation, saying tackling crime remained a priority. The killing has again drawn attention to violent crime in South Africa, where armed robberies and vehicle hijackings remain a major concern. The latest national police figures, covering April to June 2026, recorded more than 5,000 murders and close to 4,000 carjackings. When releasing the figures last month, acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said serious crimes continued to create fear in communities and that some were carried out by "organised, heavily armed criminal groups that operate with planning and sophistication".

schema.headline: Owen Ndlovu: Abducted South African journalist found dead with gunshot wounds

title: Wife of US scholar jailed in China asks Trump raise arrest at Xi meeting
description: The wife of a US scholar imprisoned in China on charges of spying and endangering national security has asked President Donald Trump to secure his rel
body: The wife of a US scholar imprisoned in China on charges of spying and endangering national security has asked President Donald Trump to secure his release when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House next week. U Min Zin, the director at a think tank focused on Myanmar, was arrested on 3 June after travelling to the Chinese city of Kunming for an academic conference. "I'm deeply hopeful that President Trump will raise my husband's case with President Xi Jinping at the summit next week," his wife, Sylvia Zin, testified to Congress on Wednesday.Xi is due to arrive for a state visit to Washington DC on Wednesday. It comes after Xi hosted Trump for a visit to Beijing in May. Ahead of the meeting, families of prisoners being held in China have travelled to the US capital to advocate for their release. Sylvia Zin appeared before the House Foreign Affairs Committee East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee on Wednesday for a hearing titled Lives, Not Leverage: The Long Arm of China and North Korea's Repression.In her remarks, Zin said she believed Trump would also be able to secure the release of Chen Youlin, a US seismologist who tracks nuclear tests that has been held in prison in China for two years."Knowing the president's historic record on bringing wrongfully detained Americans home has reassured me that he will also be able to secure the swift release of Min Zin and other wrongfully detained citizens," she said.Congresswoman Young Kim, the chairwoman of the subcommittee, opened the hearing by warning Americans: "If you travel to China, Beijing may take you hostage as leverage in diplomatic negotiation."Speaking about Zin's arrest, she added: "Beijing wanted to send a message to those whose research inconvenienced it, and detained Mr Zin ahead of the upcoming Trump-Xi summit."Min Zin, a student activist during Myanmar's 1988 pro-democracy movement, directs the Myanmar Institute for Strategic and Policy Studies (ISP-Myanmar), a think tank that studies China's role in Myanmar, including Chinese interests, relations, and regional influence.The son of Hong Kong media mogul Jimmy Lai also appeared on Capitol Hill to call on Trump to secure his father's release. The US president previously raised the case with Xi, telling reporters that his Chinese counterpart "told me that would be a tough one".Asked for comment on Thursday, a senior White House official, speaking anonymously, told the BBC: "Resolving the wrongful detentions of US citizens is always a top priority for the President." Last month, the US State Department said that two Americans - U Min Zin and Chen Youlin - were being "wrongfully detained" in China. This designation in the US allows the cases to be transferred to the office of the Special Envoy for Hostage Affairs - raising the profile of each case and allowing the US government to allocate more resources to securing their release.Zin, who lives in Thailand, told the committee on Wednesday that she has not yet been able to speak to her husband in jail, "so every month, we anxiously await his consular visits because they reassure us that he is alive".Zin said US officials had told her that Min Zin was being subjected to up to six hours of interrogations each day when he first arrived in jail. "I'm trying to be strong for our daughter, but I'm constantly wondering if he's OK and how to get him back home to us," she said.Last time Trump and Xi formally met, Trump pressed for the return of another American in jail. Underground church leader Jin Mingri was freed two months after Trump's request.

schema.headline: Wife of US scholar jailed in China asks Trump raise arrest at Xi meeting

title: Eight German state premiers back Merz amid speculation over his future
description: The leaders of eight German states have backed the nation's chancellor amid growing speculation about his political future.The premiers - all of whom
body: The leaders of eight German states have backed the nation's chancellor amid growing speculation about his political future.The premiers - all of whom are part of Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) - wrote that restoring trust in their party lay in "listening ​and taking political action, not in debates ​over personnel".Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months, is facing poor approval ratings while the anti-immigration, far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is surging, prompting questions about whether he is an electoral liability.He has vowed to carry on but two more state elections on Sunday have been seen as a key test of his leadership.Rumours of a "Kanzlertausch" - or "Chancellor swap" - have been around for months, but they have increased since the conservative CDU tumbled to a distant second behind the AfD in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt at the start of September.The AfD shot up to 43.8% of the vote while the CDU plummeted to 17.2%, marking the first time since World War Two that a far-right party has come close to controlling a German state.It is still three seats short of an outright majority and the major parties would not enter into a coalition with the AfD, though it could seek to form a minority government.Merz came out fighting after the loss, describing the AfD - which wants to rebuild ties with Russia - as a "destructive force" whose migration policy amounted to an "ethnic cleansing" of skilled workers.The AfD responded to his remarks by saying it was filing a defamation complaint against the chancellor over what it described as "baseless" and "disgusting" claims.The chancellor's abrasive communication style and personal unpopularity - with just 14% thinking he is right for the job, according to a recent Bild poll - have raised questions about his viability as leader of both Germany and the CDU.The CDU's eight state premiers wrote, however, that "now more than ever, ⁠Germany's political landscape needs stability"."Our country will continue to need a stable and effective federal government with its own majority in the Bundestag [German parliament]," said the leaders of Schleswig-Holstein, Saxony, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, Berlin and North Rhine-Westphalia.It comes after Markus Söder, the premier of Bavaria and leader of the CDU's sister party the CSU, stood by Merz.An unnamed party source told news agency Reuters that CDU officials will meet on Sunday to co-ordinate the party's response to the results of that day's state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-West Pomerania - where the AfD is poised for further gains and the CDU for further losses.However, the race is far more evenly split in the German capital than it was in Saxony-Anhalt, with the CDU and Die Linke (The Left) vying for first place, and the AfD and Greens not far behind, according to polls.In Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, polls put the AfD ahead of the centre-left SPD but likely well short of an outright majority.The worst-case scenario for Merz would be for the CDU to lose power in Berlin and not get enough votes to even have a presence in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania's parliament.Unlike in the UK, Germany is not well-versed in replacing its leader mid-term, though Merz could, in theory, be pressured to resign or face a vote of no confidence, though many regard that outcome as unlikely.No one within the CDU has yet said they were willing to challenge Merz, but the speculation about his future has led to several names - including Söder, North Rhine-Westphalia premier Hendrik Wüst and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt - being touted as potential successors.Even before Merz had officially been made chancellor, he managed to rally support for a massive €500bn ($547bn; £420bn) defence infrastructure fund, with his straight-talking style and focus on European security earning him plaudits on the world stage.But it took him three attempts to become CDU leader and he then lost an initial vote to become chancellor despite technically having sufficient votes through a coalition deal with the SPD. It was a first in post-war Germany.This suggests that he has a history of struggling to appeal to even those within his own ranks - and that he may be unlikely to let go of a job he has long coveted.

schema.headline: Eight German state premiers back Merz amid speculation over his future

title: Jurgen Klopp: New Germany coach wants to 'reclaim' flag amid elections
description: New Germany coach Jurgen Klopp says his team can help ensure "national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people" after a recent far-right election v
body: New Germany coach Jurgen Klopp says his team can help ensure "national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people" after a recent far-right election victory.The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, falling just short of securing an absolute majority in the regional parliament.The anti-immigration party also expects strong results in elections on Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.Speaking at a news conference to announce his first squad, Klopp stressed he is not a political "expert" but added: "We had an election where some people may have thought it was OK, while others were saying, 'my God, what is happening here?'"From my perspective as a sportsman, I can say that I would very much like to reclaim the flag for myself, for all of us."I want it so that when someone waves it, no one thinks: 'What is wrong with you?' Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country."No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, when the ruling Nazi party carried out the Holocaust."I do not want to entrust national pride to the wrong people," said Klopp, who prefers the term "positive patriotism" to "national pride", which he fears can be misunderstood.The former Liverpool boss added: "I can be proud to be German while also being open-minded and diverse, and kind and friendly."Klopp also said it was more important that the country had enough doctors and caregivers but said football can "foster a sense of community, so that people can truly feel the power of sport".

schema.headline: Jurgen Klopp: New Germany coach wants to 'reclaim' flag amid elections
